intro: Eight tasks on experimental work: two experiment plans, assessing a report, measurement data as a graph, a calculation task with uncertainties and a task that combines modules.

tasks.title: Grip of indoor sports shoes
tasks.text: A floorball club wants to know whether a new indoor shoe grips the hall floor better than the old model. The coach gives you one shoe of each model and a piece of the same floor material as in the hall (a board, $1.2\,\text{m} \cdot 0.30\,\text{m}$). You also have a spring balance (range $0\text{–}20\,\text{N}$, scale division $0.2\,\text{N}$), a set of masses, a kitchen scale (resolution $1\,\text{g}$), a tape measure and a phone whose inclinometer has a resolution of $0.1^\circ$.

parts.text: Plan an experiment to compare the grip of the shoes. Say what you measure and with which instrument, how the measurement is done, what you keep constant and how many measurements you make.
hints: Which single number do you compare for the grip of the shoes, when the shoes have different masses? Which phenomenon tells you when a shoe is still not sliding?
For static friction, $F_{\mu 0} \le \mu_0 N$ holds. How can you measure this limit with a board, a spring balance and a tilt meter?

Write four items into the plan: what you measure and with which instrument, how the measurement is done, what you keep constant and how many repeats you make. What must stay the same between the shoe and the board?

criteria.text: Chooses the coefficient of static friction as the measure of grip and justifies why the coefficient and not just the force: the shoes have different weights.

Describes the measurement so that it can be repeated: the board is tilted slowly until the shoe starts to slide, and the angle is read, or the shoe is pulled along the horizontal board with the spring balance and the reading is taken just before it starts to move.
Names the things kept constant: the same board and the same spot on it, a clean and dry surface, the same mass inside the shoe and the same way of tilting or pulling.
Repeats the measurement several times with each shoe, for example five times in turn.

parts.text: How do you calculate the result from your measurements, and how do you show that the difference between the shoes is real and not variation in the measurements?
hints: Which quantity do your measurements give directly, and which quantity do you calculate from them? How does one measurement become a number for grip?
When tilting, the limit of sliding is the limit of static friction, $\mu_0 N$. Which forces are then in balance along the board? When pulling, the limit is also $\mu_0 N$, where $N = mg$.
For each shoe, calculate the mean and half the range. How do the two intervals look on a number line if the difference is real, and how if it is not?

criteria.detail: When tilting, $\mu_0 = \tan\alpha_0$; when pulling, $\mu_0 = \tfrac{F}{mg}$, with the mass of the shoe and the mass weighed.
For each shoe, the mean and the error estimate as half the range.
The difference is probably real if the uncertainty intervals do not overlap; if they do, the difference cannot be shown.

parts.text: Name two significant sources of error and say how you reduce the effect of each.
hints: At which step of the measurement can a reading go wrong or the grip of the shoe change? Which of them would affect the result most?
Describe a source of error by saying in which direction it changes the reading and whether it is random or always in the same direction.
For each source of error, write a chain of three parts: the source, the direction in which it changes the reading, and what you do to reduce it.

criteria.detail: Two real sources of error and the effect of each, for example: fast tilting or a jerky pull gives too large a reading; dust or moisture changes the friction; the reading of the spring balance fluctuates as the motion begins.

criteria.text: Gives a way to reduce each source of error, for example slow and steady tilting, wiping the surface before every measurement, measuring the shoes in turn and zeroing the balance.

tasks.title: Heating rapeseed oil
tasks.text: A home economics teacher claims that rapeseed oil heats up faster than water with the same power, because the specific heat capacity of oil is smaller. You have an insulated vacuum flask with a lid, an electric heating resistor with a power of $50\,\text{W}$, a digital thermometer (resolution $0.1\,{}^\circ\text{C}$), a balance (resolution $0.1\,\text{g}$), a stopwatch, a stirrer, rapeseed oil and water.

parts.text: Plan an experiment to determine the specific heat capacity of rapeseed oil. Say what you measure and how, and what you keep constant.
hints: How much thermal energy does the heater give in a given time, and which measurement tells you where this energy goes? Which quantities do you therefore need?
The energy from the heater is $E = Pt$, and it warms the liquid: $Pt = cm\,\Delta T$. Which quantities of the equation do you already know, and which must you measure?
Write into the plan what you weigh, what you measure and how often, and what you keep constant. What would you find out if you made the same measurement with another liquid?

criteria.text: Weighs the oil on the balance, for example about $200\,\text{g}$, and records the power of the resistor.
Measures the temperature at regular intervals, for example every $30\,\text{s}$, stirring all the time, and records the times and temperatures in a table.
Keeps the conditions constant: the same container and lid, an initial temperature close to room temperature, steady stirring and a temperature rise of at most about $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$.
Makes the same measurement with water, so that the claim can be compared and the effect of the container's own heat capacity can be estimated.

parts.text: How is the specific heat capacity determined from a graph of the measurements?
hints: What does the graph of temperature against time look like when the power is constant and the oil is stirred? Which part of the graph fits the model best?
From $P\,\Delta t = cm\,\Delta T$ you get $\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} = \dfrac{P}{cm}$. Which property of the graph is $\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}$?
Fit a line to the part of the $(t, T)$ points that is straight, read its slope $k$ and solve for $c$ from it. Why should you not use all the data when the oil has become warmer than its surroundings?

criteria.detail: A straight line is fitted to the initial part of the $(t, T)$ graph, where the points lie on a line, and its slope $k = \tfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t}$ is read.
$P\,\Delta t = cm\,\Delta T$, so $c = \tfrac{P}{mk}$.

criteria.text: Justifies why the initial part is used: when the oil becomes warmer than its surroundings, the heat losses grow and the graph curves.

parts.text: According to a data book, the specific heat capacity of rapeseed oil is about $2.0\,\text{kJ/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$. Estimate how long it takes to heat a $200\,\text{g}$ batch of oil by $20\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ when no heat is lost.
hints: Which energy is needed to warm the oil, and what supplies it? How is the time related to these two?
The energy from the heater is $Pt$ and the energy needed to warm the oil is $cm\,\Delta T$. When no heat is lost, $Pt = cm\,\Delta T$.
Convert the units first: $200\,\text{g}$ to kilograms and $2.0\,\text{kJ/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$ to $\text{J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$. Then solve for the time $t$.

criteria.detail: $P t = cm\,\Delta T$, from which $t = \tfrac{cm\,\Delta T}{P}$.
Mass in kilograms and kilojoules in joules.
$t \approx 160\,\text{s}$, or about $2.7\,\text{min}$, two significant figures.

parts.text: Heat is lost to the surroundings during the experiment. Does the specific heat capacity come out too large or too small? Justify your answer and say how the effect is reduced.
hints: If part of the energy from the heater is lost to the surroundings, does the oil receive the energy assumed in the calculation? What does this do to the rate of temperature rise?
The result is calculated with $c = \dfrac{P}{mk}$. How does $c$ change if the real slope $k$ is smaller than in the lossless case?
Think of one measure that reduces the losses and one way in which the effect of the losses could be estimated from the measurement.

criteria.detail: The losses are a systematic error: part of the energy from the resistor does not heat the oil, so the temperature rises more slowly, the slope is too small and $c = \tfrac{P}{mk}$ too large.

criteria.text: A way to reduce the effect: a lid and insulation, a short measurement and using only the initial part of the graph, or alternatively an initial temperature a few degrees below room temperature and a line fitted to the whole measurement; the effect of the container and the losses can also be found with the same measurement using water.

tasks.title: Report on a drop experiment
tasks.source_note: The report and its measurement results are an invented example.
tasks.text:
From a student pair's report:

> **Research question:** How large is the free-fall acceleration?
>
> **Hypothesis:** The free-fall acceleration is $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$.
>
> **Method:** We dropped a tennis ball from the school balcony. The height was measured with a tape measure, and it was $3.0\,\text{m}$. One of us dropped the ball, and the other timed it with a phone stopwatch. We repeated this three times.
>
> **Results:** $t_1 = 0.82\,\text{s}$, $t_2 = 0.75\,\text{s}$ and $t_3 = 0.79\,\text{s}$. The mean is $\bar{t} = 0.7867\,\text{s}$. With the formula $g = \tfrac{2h}{t^2}$ we got $g = 9.6955\,\text{m/s}^2$.
>
> **Conclusion:** The result is almost $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$, so the hypothesis was proved correct. The small difference is due to air resistance.

parts.text: Assess the report. Present at least four shortcomings and justify why each weakens the result or the conclusion.
hints: Read the report as an inspector: could another group repeat the experiment from it? What is missing from the result for it to be compared with $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$?

Look at three things: the accuracy of the timing compared with a time of about $0.8\,\text{s}$, the number of digits in the result, and what the words ‘was proved’ and ‘is caused by air resistance’ would require.

Think how large a part of a time of about $0.8\,\text{s}$ the reaction time is when the timing is done by hand. Is the difference between the result and $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ larger or smaller than the uncertainty of the measurement?

criteria.detail: The result lacks an uncertainty, and it has too many digits: $9.6955$ claims a precision that the measurement does not support.

criteria.text: The reaction time of timing by hand, about $0.1\,\text{s}$, is a large part of the fall time of about $0.8\,\text{s}$, and when the person dropping and the person timing are different people, the starting moment is uncertain. Three repetitions from one height are not enough.

criteria.detail: The claim about air resistance is unjustified: the difference from $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ is smaller than the timing uncertainty, so the measurement cannot show an effect of air resistance.
A measurement cannot prove a hypothesis; it can only support it within its uncertainty.

criteria.text: The method does not say from where to where the height was measured (from the bottom of the ball to the floor) or to what precision, so the experiment cannot be repeated exactly.

parts.text: Determine the free-fall acceleration and its uncertainty from the report's measurements with the extreme-value method.
hints: The ball starts from rest. Which equation gives the acceleration of free fall from the height and the time? Which measurement affects the result most?
When the ball starts from rest, $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, so $g = \dfrac{2h}{t^2}$. In the extreme-value method the uncertainty is half the difference between the largest and the smallest result.

Calculate $g$ both with the shortest time $0.75\,\text{s}$ and with the longest time $0.82\,\text{s}$, using the height $3.0\,\text{m}$. Which time gives the larger $g$? Round the result to the same decimal as the uncertainty.

criteria.detail: The ball starts from rest: $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$, from which $g = \tfrac{2h}{t^2}$.
$g_\text{max}$ with the shortest time $0.75\,\text{s}$ and $g_\text{min}$ with the longest time $0.82\,\text{s}$.
$\Delta g = \tfrac{g_\text{max} - g_\text{min}}{2} \approx 0.9\,\text{m/s}^2$.
$g = (9.7 \pm 0.9)\,\text{m/s}^2$: the result is rounded to the same decimal place as the error estimate.

parts.text: Suggest an improved method using ordinary school equipment. Also say how the result is calculated.
hints: Which part of the report's measurement caused the greatest uncertainty? How could it be removed or reduced with school equipment?
Instead of repeating one height, you can measure at several heights. Which quantities on the axes make $h = \tfrac{1}{2}gt^2$ a straight line, and what does its slope tell you?

Write into the method how you get the time without timing by hand, how many heights you use and how many repeats of each. Then calculate the quantity of the horizontal axis for each height and fit a line.

criteria.text: Timing without reaction time: the drop is filmed with a phone in front of a tape measure and the time is read from the frames, or light gates are used.
Several drop heights, with repetitions at each.

criteria.detail: A line through the origin is fitted to the $(t^2, h)$ graph, and its slope is $\tfrac{g}{2}$; or a $(t, v)$ graph is drawn from the video, and its slope is $g$.

tasks.title: Length and period of a pendulum
tasks.source_note: The data have been calculated from the pendulum model, with small random variation added as in a measurement. They are not the result of a real measurement.
tasks.text:
A group measured the period of a pendulum with six string lengths. The pendulum was a steel ball on the end of a thin string, and the starting angle was about $5^\circ$ in all measurements. The length $l$ was measured with a tape measure from the point where the string is fixed to the top of the ball. For each length, the time $t_{10}$ of ten swings was measured three times, and the table gives their mean.

| $l\ (\text{m})$ | $t_{10}\ (\text{s})$ |
|---|---|
| $0.250$ | $10.55$ |
| $0.400$ | $13.04$ |
| $0.550$ | $15.23$ |
| $0.700$ | $17.06$ |
| $0.850$ | $18.81$ |
| $1.000$ | $20.28$ |

parts.text: Draw a graph of the measurements from which the free-fall acceleration can be determined, and fit a straight line to the points.
hints: What is the relation between the period and the length of a pendulum? Which quantities on the axes should put the points on a straight line?
Square the model $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g}}$. To which quantity is $T^2$ directly proportional?
The table gives the time of ten swings. For each row calculate the period $T = t_{10} : 10$ and then $T^2$. Plot the points and fit a line between them.

criteria.text: Chooses the quantities $l$ and $T^2$ and justifies the choice: the pendulum model $T^2 = \tfrac{4\pi^2}{g}\, l$ is the equation of a straight line.

criteria.detail: $T = t_{10} : 10$ and $T^2$ for each row, for example $l = 0.250\,\text{m}$: $T^2 = 1.113\,\text{s}^2$.
The line runs among the points and is not forced through the origin.

parts.text: Determine the free-fall acceleration from the graph.
hints: Which property of the graph is related to the acceleration of free fall? Why is it best to read the slope from two points of the line that are far apart?
Compare the model $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}\,l$ with the equation of a line $y = kx + b$. How are the slope $k$ and $g$ related?
Read two points far apart on the line and calculate $k = \dfrac{\Delta (T^2)}{\Delta l}$. Then solve $g$ from the equation.

criteria.detail: The slope is read from two points of the line far apart: $k \approx 4.0\,\text{s}^2/\text{m}$.
$k = \tfrac{4\pi^2}{g}$, from which $g = \tfrac{4\pi^2}{k}$.
$g \approx 9.8\,\text{m/s}^2$.

parts.text: The line does not pass through the origin. Explain what causes the constant term, and use the graph to determine the diameter of the ball.
hints: What does $l$ stand for in the pendulum model? From which point to which point did the group measure the length?
If the model is $T^2 = \dfrac{4\pi^2}{g}(l + r)$, where $r$ is the distance that was left unmeasured, expand the brackets and compare with the equation of a line $y = kx + b$.
Read the constant term $b$ from the point where the line crosses the vertical axis. Which equation gives $r$ when you know $k$ and $b$? What is the diameter once you know $r$?

criteria.text: Explains the constant term: the length of the pendulum is from the fixing point to the centre of the ball, so each measured length lacks the radius $r$ of the ball, and the model is $T^2 = \tfrac{4\pi^2}{g}(l + r)$.

criteria.detail: The constant term is read where the line cuts the vertical axis: $b \approx 0.10\,\text{s}^2$.
$b = kr$, so $r = \tfrac{b}{k}$, or the extension of the line cuts the horizontal axis at $l = -r$.
$r \approx 2.5\,\text{cm}$ and diameter $d \approx 5\,\text{cm}$.

parts.text: Assess how the error in measuring the length affected the result of part b and how it would have affected it if $g$ had been calculated from each row separately. Is the result consistent with the value $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$?
hints: The error in the length is systematic. What happens to the line if the same distance is added to every length? Which property of the line changes and which stays the same?
In the calculation row by row, $g = \dfrac{4\pi^2 l}{T^2}$, the length is included directly. How large is the relative effect of the same length error with a short string and with a long string?

Calculate $g$ from the first row of the table ($l = 0.250\,\text{m}$, $T = 1.055\,\text{s}$). Then estimate the uncertainty of reading the slope and its effect on $g$. Is $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ within the uncertainty interval of the result?

criteria.detail: A systematic error in the length shifts the line but does not change the slope, so $g$ in part b is not distorted.

criteria.text: A row-by-row $g = \tfrac{4\pi^2 l}{T^2}$ would be too small on every row and most so with a short string: $l = 0.250\,\text{m}$ gives about $8.9\,\text{m/s}^2$.

criteria.detail: The uncertainty in reading the slope is about $\pm 0.1\,\text{s}^2/\text{m}$, so $g = (9.8 \pm 0.3)\,\text{m/s}^2$, and the value $9.81\,\text{m/s}^2$ is within the interval.

tasks.title: Density of a beach stone
tasks.source_note: The measurement results are an invented example; the densities of the rock types are typical table values.
tasks.text:
In a geology club a student wants to identify a stone she found on the beach by its density. She weighs the stone on a digital balance with a resolution of $0.1\,\text{g}$ and gets $187.4\,\text{g}$. Then she lowers the stone into a $250\,\text{m}\textsf{l}$ measuring cylinder whose scale division is $2\,\text{m}\textsf{l}$. The water level rises from the reading $120\,\text{m}\textsf{l}$ to the reading $190\,\text{m}\textsf{l}$. She estimates the uncertainty of each reading as half a scale division and the uncertainty of the balance reading as $0.1\,\text{g}$.

According to a data book, the density of granite is typically $2600\text{–}2800\,\text{kg/m}^3$ and that of basalt $2800\text{–}3000\,\text{kg/m}^3$.

parts.text: Calculate the density of the stone.
hints: How is density defined, and which two quantities do you get from the measurements? Where does the volume come from when the stone is in the measuring cylinder?
Density is $\rho = \dfrac{m}{V}$, where $V$ is the volume of water displaced by the stone, that is, the difference of the two readings of the water level.
Remember that $1\,\text{m}\textsf{l} = 1\,\text{cm}^3$ and $1\,\text{g/cm}^3 = 1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$. Calculate $V$ first, then $\rho$, and think how many significant figures the result can have.

criteria.detail: $\rho = \tfrac{m}{V}$, where $V = V_2 - V_1$ is the volume of water displaced by the stone.
$V = 70\,\text{m}\textsf{l} = 70\,\text{cm}^3$ and $\rho = 2.677\,\text{g/cm}^3$.
$1\,\text{g/cm}^3 = 1000\,\text{kg/m}^3$, so $\rho \approx 2.7 \cdot 10^3\,\text{kg/m}^3$, two significant figures as in the volume $70\,\text{cm}^3$; $2680\,\text{kg/m}^3$ is also accepted.

parts.text: Determine the uncertainty of the density with the extreme-value method.
hints: Which of the numbers of the measurements may be off, and by how much? With which combination of mass and volume is the density greatest and with which smallest?

The volume is the difference of two readings, so its uncertainty is the sum of the uncertainties of the readings. In the extreme-value method $\Delta\rho = \dfrac{\rho_\text{max} - \rho_\text{min}}{2}$.
First write the extreme values of $m$ and $V$ with the uncertainties of the task. Calculate $\rho_\text{max}$ and $\rho_\text{min}$ from them and then half their difference.

criteria.text: The uncertainty of the volume is the sum of the uncertainties of the two readings: $\Delta V = 2 \cdot 1\,\text{m}\textsf{l} = 2\,\text{m}\textsf{l}$.

criteria.detail: Largest density with the largest mass and the smallest volume: $\rho_\text{max} = \tfrac{187.5\,\text{g}}{68\,\text{cm}^3}$ and $\rho_\text{min} = \tfrac{187.3\,\text{g}}{72\,\text{cm}^3}$.
$\Delta\rho = \tfrac{\rho_\text{max} - \rho_\text{min}}{2} \approx 80\,\text{kg/m}^3$.

parts.text: Can the stone be identified as granite or basalt by its density?
hints: Within which interval can the density of the stone lie when the uncertainty is taken into account? Which ranges of the table book does this interval fall into?
Compare the lower and upper limit of the result interval with the limits of the ranges of granite and basalt. What does the interval allow, and what does it rule out?
Think also whether one quantity is enough to identify a rock: is the range in the table one rock or a typical value, and can another rock have the same density?

criteria.detail: The interval $2600\text{–}2760\,\text{kg/m}^3$ is in the range of granite, and the lower limit of basalt, $2800\,\text{kg/m}^3$, is outside the interval, so the result supports granite.

criteria.text: States that density alone does not prove the rock type: the ranges in the table are typical values, and other rock types can have the same density.

parts.text: Which measurement limits the precision of the result more, the mass or the volume? Suggest how the result could be made more precise.
hints: How do you compare the importance of two measurements when they have different units and different sizes? Which number tells how large a part of the measurement the uncertainty is?
The relative uncertainty is $\dfrac{\Delta x}{x}$. Calculate it for the mass and for the volume with the readings of the task.
Compare the relative uncertainties: reducing which one would improve the result most? Think how its measurement could be made more precise, and estimate what new uncertainty that brings.

criteria.detail: Relative uncertainties: mass $0.1 : 187.4 \approx 0.05\,\%$ and volume $2 : 70 \approx 3\,\%$, so the volume is the limit.

criteria.text: Suggests a way to reduce the uncertainty of the volume and assesses its real precision: a narrower measuring cylinder with a smaller scale division, or an overflow can whose water is weighed (the weighing is precise, but the water left in the can and the spout brings an uncertainty of about $0.5\,\text{cm}^3$). Air bubbles are removed from the surface of the stone.

tasks.title: Braking distance of a bicycle
tasks.source_note: The data have been calculated from the model of constant deceleration, with small random variation added as in a measurement. They are not the result of a real measurement.
tasks.text:
In a road safety project, students investigated the braking distance of a bicycle on dry asphalt. The cyclist rode up to the start line at a steady speed shown by a phone app and braked at the line with both brakes so that the wheels did not lock. The braking distance $s$ was measured with a tape measure from the line to the stopping point. The road was horizontal, and there was no wind.

| $v\ (\text{km/h})$ | $s\ (\text{m})$ |
|---|---|
| $10$ | $1.0$ |
| $15$ | $2.0$ |
| $20$ | $3.8$ |
| $25$ | $5.6$ |
| $30$ | $8.5$ |

parts.text: The students assume that the deceleration is the same in every braking. What does the assumption predict about the relationship between the braking distance and the speed, and with what kind of graph can the assumption be tested?
hints: If the deceleration is constant, what kind of motion is it? Which equation connects the velocity, the deceleration and the distance without the time?
For a bicycle that decelerates uniformly to a stop, $v^2 = 2as$. Solve $s$ from this and see how $s$ depends on the velocity $v$.
What happens to the braking distance when the velocity doubles? Choose as axes the quantities for which the dependence is a straight line. Where does the line go when the velocity is zero?

criteria.detail: In uniformly decelerated motion $v^2 = 2as$, so $s = \tfrac{v^2}{2a}$.

criteria.text: Prediction: doubling the speed quadruples the braking distance.
Test: the $(v^2, s)$ graph is a straight line through the origin if the assumption holds.

parts.text: Draw a graph with which you test the assumption, and determine the deceleration of the bicycle from it.
hints: Which quantities plotted make the relation between the braking distance and the velocity a straight line? In which units must they be?
The assumption gives $s = \dfrac{v^2}{2a}$. Compare with the equation of a line $y = kx$ and decide what the slope $k$ is and how it is related to $a$.
Convert the velocities first to $\text{m/s}$ (for example $10\,\text{km/h} \approx 2.8\,\text{m/s}$) and only then square them. Read the slope from two points of the line that are far apart.

criteria.detail: $v^2$ in $\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2$ on the horizontal axis, $s$ in $\text{m}$ on the vertical axis.
The speeds have been converted to $\text{m/s}$ before squaring.
The points are close to a straight line through the origin, so the assumption is supported; the line passes through the origin because at zero speed the braking distance is zero.
Slope $k \approx 0.12\,\text{s}^2/\text{m}$ from a distant point of the line.
$k = \tfrac{1}{2a}$, so $a = \tfrac{1}{2k} \approx 4.2\,\text{m/s}^2$.

parts.text: How large must the coefficient of static friction between the tyres and the asphalt be at least for such braking to be possible? Air resistance is not taken into account.
hints: Which force decelerates the bicycle on a horizontal road? Is the tyre sliding relative to the road or not, and which friction is it then?
In the horizontal direction only friction decelerates: $ma = F_{\mu 0}$, and for static friction $F_{\mu 0} \le \mu_0 N$.

Substitute $N = mg$ and cancel the mass. What condition remains for $\mu_0$ when you use the deceleration of part b? Think whether the asked value is an upper or a lower limit, and what the unit of the coefficient is.

criteria.text: Justifies that the bicycle is slowed by the friction force of the road on the tyres and that the wheels do not slip, so this is static friction: $F_{\mu 0} \le \mu_0 N$, where $N = mg$.

criteria.detail: $ma = F_{\mu 0} \le \mu_0 mg$, so $\mu_0 \ge \tfrac{a}{g}$.
$\mu_0 \ge 0.42$, without a unit.

parts.text: It later turned out that the app showed the speed $5\,\%$ higher than the true speed in every run. By how many per cent does the deceleration of part b differ from the true value, and in which direction? Does the conclusion that the deceleration is constant change?
hints: The app shows all velocities too large in the same proportion. What does this do to the quantity of the horizontal axis and to the slope?
If $v_\text{app} = 1.05\,v$, express $v_\text{app}^2$ with $v^2$. How do the slope $k$ and the deceleration $a = \dfrac{1}{2k}$ change?
First decide whether the slope grows or shrinks when $v^2$ grows. Then calculate by how many percent $1.05^2$ is above $1$. Do the points stay on a line?

criteria.text: Identifies the error as systematic: every speed has been multiplied by the same number $1.05$.

criteria.detail: $v_\text{app}^2 = 1.05^2\, v^2$, so the slope is $1.05^2$ times too small and $a = \tfrac{1}{2k}$ is $1.05^2$ times too large.
$1.05^2 = 1.1025$: the deceleration is about $10\,\%$ too large, the true value about $3.8\,\text{m/s}^2$.
Every $v^2$ changes in the same proportion, so the points stay on a straight line and the conclusion about constant deceleration does not change.

tasks.title: Measuring sliding friction
tasks.source_note: The situation and the measurement data are invented examples.
tasks.text: A group measured the sliding friction force $F_\mu$ of a wooden block on a table at several values of the normal force $N$. The block was pulled horizontally at a constant speed with a spring balance, and the normal force was changed by placing masses on the block. The scale division of the spring balance is $0.1\,\text{N}$. The graph shows the measurement points.

parts.text: Examine the graph. Is there any sign of a systematic error in the data? What does the graph tell about random variation?
hints: Look at how the points lie around the line and where the line meets the vertical axis. What different kinds of errors can be read from the graph?
A systematic error moves all points in the same direction, random variation scatters the points on both sides of the line. What does the line's passing through the origin tell you?

Estimate how much the points deviate vertically from the line and compare the deviation with the scale interval of the spring balance, $0.1\,\text{N}$. Do the points deviate in one direction or in both?

criteria.text: States that the points lie close to a straight line through the origin, so the friction force is directly proportional to the normal force: $F_\mu = \mu N$.

Concludes that the graph shows no systematic error: the line is not shifted along the vertical axis. For example, a wrongly zeroed spring balance would move all the points up or down by the same amount.
States that the points deviate from the line by about $0.1\,\text{N}$ or less, sometimes up and sometimes down, and regards this as random variation.

parts.text: Determine the coefficient of sliding friction and its error estimate from the graph.
hints: Which property of the graph tells the ratio of the friction force to the normal force? How can the error estimate be found from several points?
For sliding friction $F_\mu = \mu N$, so the slope of the line in the $(N, F_\mu)$ graph is $\mu$. The error estimate is half the range.
Read the slope from a fitted line, or calculate the ratio $F_\mu : N$ for each point. Estimate the error as half the range of the ratios.

criteria.detail: The normal force and the friction force of each point are read from the graph: $(5\,\text{N};\ 1.1\,\text{N})$, $(10\,\text{N};\ 2.1\,\text{N})$, $(15\,\text{N};\ 3.3\,\text{N})$, $(20\,\text{N};\ 4.2\,\text{N})$ and $(25\,\text{N};\ 5.4\,\text{N})$.
$F_\mu = \mu N$, so $\mu = \dfrac{F_\mu}{N}$, the slope of the line in the graph.
The ratios $F_\mu : N$ of the points are $0.22$, $0.21$, $0.22$, $0.21$ and $0.216$, so the mean is $0.215$. The slope of a fitted line, $0.21\text{–}0.22$, is also accepted.
The error estimate is half the range, $\dfrac{0.22 - 0.21}{2} = 0.005$, so $\mu = 0.215 \pm 0.005$. An estimate of $\pm 0.01$ from extreme lines is also accepted.

parts.text: Another group used the same block and table, but their spring balance read $0.3\,\text{N}$ with no load, and the group did not take it into account. When the normal force was $10\,\text{N}$, the balance read $2.4\,\text{N}$. Calculate the coefficient of friction the group got from this reading, the correct coefficient and the size of the error as a percentage of the correct value. Also justify how the zero error would affect the slope if the coefficient were determined from a line fitted to the whole series.
hints: The spring balance shows $0.3\,\text{N}$ when unloaded. Is this reading part of the friction force? Which part of the reading is the real friction force?

The real friction force is the reading minus the zero error: $F_\mu = F_\text{reading} - F_0$, and $\mu = \dfrac{F_\mu}{N}$. What does a zero error do to the line when every point is shifted by the same amount?
Calculate the coefficient first from the uncorrected reading and then from the force corrected for the zero error. Compare the difference with the correct value in percent.

criteria.detail: The correct friction force is the reading minus the zero error, $F_\mu = F_\text{reading} - F_0$, and $\mu = \dfrac{F_\mu}{N}$.
The group's coefficient is $\dfrac{2.4\,\text{N}}{10\,\text{N}} = 0.24$ and the correct one $\dfrac{2.4\,\text{N} - 0.3\,\text{N}}{10\,\text{N}} = 0.21$.
The error is $\dfrac{0.24 - 0.21}{0.21} \approx 14\,\%$ of the correct value.

criteria.text: Explains: a zero error shifts every point vertically by the same amount, so the slope $\dfrac{\Delta F}{\Delta N}$ does not change. Only the intercept on the vertical axis changes.

parts.text: Evaluate the measurement method: name two things that weaken the reliability of the result and say how the experiment would be improved.
hints: Go through the experiment step by step: pulling, reading the value, number of repeats, surface. Where can the result vary or be distorted?
Compare the scale interval of the spring balance, $0.1\,\text{N}$, with the smallest friction force in the graph. What does it do to the point with a small normal force?
Choose two weaknesses and write a chain for each: the weakness, its effect on the result, and what you would do differently.

criteria.detail: Two real weaknesses and their effect, for example: the pulling speed is not exactly constant, so the balance reading fluctuates; there is only one measurement at each normal force; the scale division $0.1\,\text{N}$ makes the relative error large at a small normal force ($0.05\,\text{N} : 1.1\,\text{N} \approx 5\,\%$ at $N = 5\,\text{N}$); dust or moisture on the table.

criteria.text: Gives an improvement for each weakness, for example: repeat each measurement three times and take the mean, use a force sensor or a steady pulling device, add measurement points and widen the range of the normal force, wipe the table before measuring.

tasks.title: The magnetic field of a coil and sources of error
tasks.source_note: The situation and the measurement data are invented examples.
tasks.text: A group studied the magnetic field of a long air-core coil. A magnetic field sensor was placed at the centre of the coil, and the current $I$ of the coil was varied with a power supply. The graph shows the magnetic flux density $B$ measured by the sensor and a line fitted to the measurement points. The turn density of the coil, the number of turns per unit length, is $n$, and at the centre of the coil $B = \mu_0 n I$, where $\mu_0 = 4\pi \cdot 10^{-7}\,\text{Vs/(Am)}$.

parts.text: Determine the slope of the line in the graph and use it to find the turn density $n$ of the coil.
hints: Which property of the graph tells how much the field increases when the current increases? How do you read it from the graph?
Compare the model $B = \mu_0 n I$ with the equation of a line $B = kI$. How are the slope $k$ and the turn density $n$ related?
Read two points far apart on the fitted line. Convert millitesla to tesla ($1\,\text{mT} = 10^{-3}\,\text{T}$) before solving $n$.

criteria.detail: The slope is read from two points of the fitted line that are far apart, for example $(1.0\,\text{A};\ 2.5\,\text{mT})$ and $(2.5\,\text{A};\ 6.2\,\text{mT})$.
$B = \mu_0 n I$, so the slope of the line is $k = \mu_0 n$ and $n = \dfrac{k}{\mu_0}$.
The millitesla is converted to tesla. The slope has two significant figures, so $n \approx 2.0 \cdot 10^{3}\,\text{1/m}$, about $20$ turns per centimetre.

parts.text: The group wants to produce a field $B = 12\,\text{mT}$ at the centre of the coil. What current is needed according to the graph? Is the result reliable?
hints: What does the line tell about the relation of $B$ and $I$? How far from the measured current range is the required value?
The line passes practically through the origin, so $B = kI$ and $I = \dfrac{B}{k}$. What is the slope $k$ from part a?
Use the same units as in the slope and calculate the current. Compare the result with the largest measured current and think what that does to the reliability of the result.

criteria.detail: $B = kI$ and the line passes practically through the origin, so $I = \dfrac{B}{k}$.
$I = \dfrac{12\,\text{mT}}{2.47\,\text{mT/A}} \approx 4.9\,\text{A}$

criteria.text: Notes that the result is extrapolation: the largest measured current was $2.5\,\text{A}$ and the needed current is about twice that. The coil and the power supply must be able to carry such a current. The result is only an estimate and must be checked by measuring.

parts.text: With no current in the coil, the sensor still showed a reading of $0.04\,\text{mT}$. Calculate what percentage this reading is of the values of the field read from the graph at the currents $0.50\,\text{A}$ and $2.5\,\text{A}$. What type of error is this, and how does it affect the slope?
hints: Does the reading $0.04\,\text{mT}$ depend on the current? Is the error always in the same direction? What does such an error look like on the graph?
The relative share is $\dfrac{\text{error}}{\text{reading}} \cdot 100\,\%$. How does a constant affect the slope $k$ of the line $B = kI + b$, and how the constant term $b$?

Read $B$ from the graph at the currents $0.50\,\text{A}$ and $2.5\,\text{A}$ and calculate the share for each. Then imagine that $0.04\,\text{mT}$ is subtracted from all points: how does the line change?

criteria.detail: Reads $B \approx 1.3\,\text{mT}$ at $I = 0.50\,\text{A}$ and $B \approx 6.2\,\text{mT}$ at $I = 2.5\,\text{A}$.
$\dfrac{0.04\,\text{mT}}{1.3\,\text{mT}} \approx 3\,\%$ and $\dfrac{0.04\,\text{mT}}{6.2\,\text{mT}} \approx 0.6\,\%$.

criteria.text: Names the error systematic: it is constant, does not depend on the current and always has the same direction. The cause can be, for example, the Earth's magnetic field or a zero error of the sensor.

States that a constant shifts all points by the same amount, so the slope does not change and only the intercept of the line on the vertical axis moves. Calculated from a single point, the error would be relatively larger at a small current.

parts.text: Evaluate the design of the experiment. Does the model $B \propto I$ fit the measurement, and how would the experiment be improved?
hints: Look at how the points lie around the line. What does that tell about whether the model $B \propto I$ fits the measured current range?
The fit of a model concerns only the measured range. Also think what systematic error there was in the experiment and how it could be measured and removed from the results.
Think of one more weakness in the implementation of the experiment (for example the number of repeats, the steadiness of the current or the position of the sensor) and one improvement for it.

criteria.text: States that the points lie almost on the line and deviate from it only a little in both directions, so the model fits the current range $0\text{–}2.5\,\text{A}$ and the random variation is small.

Says how the systematic error is removed: the zero reading is measured with no current and subtracted from all readings, or the current is reversed and $B$ is calculated as half the difference of the readings.

Names another weakness and an improvement, for example: only one reading at each current, so repeat the measurements; if the supply regulates voltage, the current may drift as the coil warms up, so read the current at every reading and keep it on only for a short time; the sensor must be at the centre of the coil.
